archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A third-year passer who works from the pocket and wins by pushing the ball 10-plus yards downfield, not with his legs or a quick short game, and who accepts long holds and sacks as the cost of that approach.

report.headline: Downfield accuracy is real now; sacks and red-zone stalls cap the ceiling.
report.take:
McCarthy arrived in this Giants season as the fourth name in a quarterback rotation. Jaxson Dart and Jameis Winston started the first six weeks, he came on in relief against New Orleans, and he has started the two games since, both wins. In 68 attempts he has looked like a different passer from the one who finished 2025 in Minnesota with a -5.7 CPOE, a 21% bad-throw rate and 12 interceptions. This year his CPOE is 4.88, seventh of 49, and his 9.15 yards per attempt ranks second. His bad-throw rate has been cut roughly in half to 10.3%, and he has thrown one interception.

Nearly all of that comes from one area of the field. On throws of 10 or more air yards he is at 1.038 EPA per attempt with a 13.3 CPOE and a 60% success rate. Under 10 air yards he is at -0.212, with screens and checkdowns behind the line among the worst of it. He is not a distributor who strings together completions. He hunts intermediate and deep throws, he is accurate on them, and Malik Nabers (0.525 EPA per target) and Isaiah Likely (0.472) are the payoff. The rest of his game is ordinary or worse. Designed runs have been dead plays, and the offense collapses under center (-0.352 EPA, 35.7% completions), which matters in a John Harbaugh offense that passes less than situation predicts (29th in pass rate over expected).

The numbers hide two costs. The first is sacks. Nine of them on 77 dropbacks gives an 11.7% sack rate, 44th of 49, and 14.5% in his two starts, including five in Philadelphia, where he lost EPA as a passer. Part of that is the price of his style: he holds the ball (2.88 seconds) waiting on routes that develop downfield. Part is context. The line ranks 30th in hits allowed, and a run-first offense leaves him in third-and-long, where his average distance to go is 9.2 and four of the nine sacks came. The second cost is finishing. He has one touchdown pass, a 1.5% TD rate that ranks 45th, and one completion on six red-zone throws. Last year he threw 11 touchdowns in 10 games, so this is more likely a small-sample drought than a trait, but deep shots don't work on a short field and the short game he would need there hasn't worked.

The direction is cautiously positive. The accuracy jump is too big to call pure noise, and it lines up with a new team and better targets, but 30 deep-and-intermediate throws at more than a point of EPA each will come down. The realistic version is an efficient, low-volume starter who completes the big throws, takes too many sacks, and should see his touchdowns start to arrive as red-zone luck evens out.

strengths.title: Accurate attacking 10-plus yards downfield
strengths.body: On throws of 10 or more air yards he completes 60% with a 13.3 CPOE and adds more than a point of EPA per attempt, which is why his yards per attempt ranks second. That production rests on accuracy rather than on low-percentage chucks, since his bad-throw rate has been halved. It will cool from this rate on 30 attempts, but the skill looks real.

strengths.title: A real accuracy leap from 2025
strengths.body: His CPOE is up 10.6 points on last season and his interceptions per game are down nearly a full pick. Last year he ranked 56th of 63 in CPOE and 58th in interceptions. A swing that large on 68 attempts needs a cause, and a new offense plus Nabers and Likely are plausible ones. Expect some give-back, but probably not all the way to last year's level.

strengths.title: Nabers as the downfield outlet
strengths.body: Nabers has drawn the most targets and produced the most value. He accounts for the bulk of McCarthy's passing EPA at 0.525 per target, with Likely close behind per target. That connection carries the offense's pass game, and as long as both are healthy it should last.

concerns.title: Sack rate is a drive killer
concerns.body: An 11.7% sack rate ranks 44th, and it is worse as a starter. This is partly the cost of holding the ball for deep routes and partly a line that ranks 30th in hits allowed. It is also partly game script, since a run-heavy offense leaves him in long third downs. In 2025 he sat 39th in pressure-to-sack rate, so some of this is who he is, not just this offense.

concerns.title: No finishing in the red zone
concerns.body: One touchdown pass and a single completion on six red-zone throws give him a TD rate near the bottom of the league. Six plays is far too few to call this a flaw, and his 2025 touchdown rate was normal. The underlying issue is that his short game, the part a compressed field demands, has been negative.

concerns.title: Under center and on designed runs
concerns.body: Under-center dropbacks have been a disaster, and his designed runs have produced nothing (-1.004 EPA, 40% stuffed). In a Harbaugh offense that leans run, that means the play-action and option looks the scheme wants aren't yet paying off. Scrambles have helped when used, but there have been only three.

trend.note: He was sharp in relief against New Orleans and efficient in Houston, then sacked five times for negative passing EPA in Philadelphia after the bye. Three real games is too few to call a direction, and the swings track sacks more than accuracy.

nextGame.headline: Depleted Washington front and a soft deep defense suit him
nextGame.body:
Washington fits his profile well. Its defense ranks 20th in EPA and 19th against deep passes but seventh against short throws. That tilt rewards exactly the 10-plus-yard throws he lives on and takes away the short game he struggles with anyway. Opposing quarterbacks have scored 18.9 PPR a game against it (28th), and offenses pass against it more than normal (third-strongest pass funnel). That could nudge even Harbaugh toward a few more dropbacks. The pass rush ranks only 23rd in both sack rate and hit rate, which is the best possible news for his main weakness.

Availability cuts both ways. McCarthy himself is questionable with a hip bruise and was limited Monday on a four-day turnaround. A sore hip on a short week could shorten his drops or limit his scrambling, and it is the main risk here. Darnell Mooney (questionable, chest) and Cam Skattebo (out) thin his supporting cast. Skattebo's absence likely means more Devin Singletary, whose targets have been negative for McCarthy. On Washington's side, interior linemen Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw are on season-ending IR and Shy Tuttle is questionable, gutting the middle of a rush that already rarely gets home. Light drizzle is in the forecast, but it shouldn't change much.

keyMatchups.title: Interior rush without Payne, Kinlaw
keyMatchups.body: Washington's sack and hit rates already rank in the bottom third, and it has lost two starting-caliber interior linemen for the year. Fewer free rushers up the middle is what a sack-prone quarterback who holds the ball needs. If he is sacked heavily here, the problem is mostly his own processing.

keyMatchups.title: Nabers and Likely against soft spots
keyMatchups.body: Washington has let lead receivers score 4.5 PPR over their averages (29th) and top tight ends 5.9 over (last in the league). Those are precisely his two most efficient targets. Treat it as context from a handful of games, not proof, but it lines up with his downfield, middle-of-field strengths.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots versus short-area stinginess
keyMatchups.body: Washington allows 0.436 EPA on deep throws (19th) but is seventh on short ones. He shouldn't try to dink his way down the field, and he hasn't. The game script fits his volume, too: it is a close-spread divisional game, and his own defense ranks fifth in success rate, so a low-scoring, run-leaning plan is likely.

nextGame.watch: Whether the hip limits his drop depth and movement. If he can't hold up long enough to wait on deep routes against a weakened rush, his main edge in this matchup disappears.

restOfSeason.body:
He holds the job now, and the profile points to a low-volume, high-efficiency starter. The run-first scheme and a defense that keeps games close will cap his attempts in the low-to-mid 20s, so his yardage stays modest even when he plays well. The downfield accuracy is the part to believe in, though not at a point of EPA per throw. The sack rate is the part to expect to persist, because it comes from his habit of holding the ball and a line that allows hits. Touchdowns are where the clearest positive regression sits: a 1.5% TD rate won't hold for a passer with his yards per attempt, and something like 150 to 240 passing yards with roughly one touchdown a game is a fair band.

The risks are physical and positional. A hip bruise on a short week could linger, and the Giants have already used three quarterbacks this year, so a bad run could reopen the job. His rushing will stay a footnote unless scrambles become more frequent, since designed runs haven't worked.
swingFactors: Hip health and how long he holds the job
Whether the deep accuracy holds as defenses adjust
Pass protection and how often he faces third-and-long

confidence.note: 68 attempts over three games, two starts, a new team and a large break from his 2025 profile.
